You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC grid instances; obey the one-action JSON protocol and infer transformations from demonstrations and feedback.
---

# Continual-ARC

1. Parse the independent instance, grid, attempt/demo caps, counters, and allowed actions. On every puzzle turn, including demo requests, reply only with exactly one permitted action JSON object; do not add analysis, commentary, or tool calls. Recheck counters before acting; never submit commentary alongside the action, even if it appears explanatory.
2. Infer the rule from exact input-output differences. Compare dimensions, color roles, object masks, counts, orientation, separators, and unchanged regions; preserve cells unless evidence supports changing them. Treat boundary lines as dividers, not automatic instructions to copy every region: identify the specific source object/pattern and the exact destinations changed in demos. For sparse colored diagonals that become a full repeating grid, test whether each diagonal encodes one residue of a periodic color sequence: index cells by `column - row` modulo the candidate period, read the marker colors at those residues, then verify the same mapping at multiple positions and across demos before filling. Check the diagonal direction and phase explicitly; do not infer a general rule from a coincidental overlap or merely replace apparent gaps.
3. When multiple rules fit, request a demo that distinguishes them, especially before the first guess or after a wrong submission. Choose what to disambiguate explicitly (e.g. copy source into adjacent panel vs all panels, reflect vs translate, or replicate across a divider vs only fill the displayed repeat). A wrong result refutes that output: compare it cell-by-cell with the proposed rule and demos, revise the hypothesis, and request another discriminating demo rather than repeating speculative variants. A demo's matching dimensions/colors alone is not sufficient; verify its exact transformation signature and which regions remain unchanged. Treat the demo as evidence about the transformation, not as a template for color substitution: derive the rule from aligned input/output cells, including background and all marker colors, and check whether the demonstrated relation actually applies to the test before constructing an output.
4. Before submitting, construct and validate the complete grid: row count, each row width, allowed colors, every changed cell, and unchanged regions. Submit only when the transformation is supported; use `finish` only after the instance is over.

# Continual-ARC instance task-876fed55 (unsolved)

## Demonstrated transformation
All three demos consistently show this operation: for every isolated pixel of a seed color within the uniform background, extend a straight line from the seed along one of the grid axes toward the nearest boundary line/segment of a different color that is present on the perimeter. The ray paints the intervening background cells with the seed's original color; replace each seed pixel itself with 4. Preserve all other cells, including background and boundary strokes. Direction depends on the available perimeter segment alignment / nearest edge-directed ray; this instance's exact lines were not confidently determined.

Evidence:
- Demo1 background 8, boundary color 2 on perimeter: sparse seeds color1 become 4 and horizontal rays paint color1 from each seed toward the right border; seeds aligned with a perimeter row segment are handled by ray. The top-left perimeter vertical 2 segment with no 1 seeds did not induce paint.
- Demo2 bg2; perimeter color9 segments (left rows1-9, right rows10-18), scattered color5 seeds. Seeds become 4, horizontal lines from left-side seeds paint color5 to the right, while right-side boundary case seeds paint toward left; rows without seeds remain unchanged. This shows ray orientation may be related to which perimeter boundary segment is their corresponding endpoint.
- Demo3 bg6; boundary color9 segments along top-right and bottom-left. Sparse color8 seeds become 4; their color8 rays extend from each seed along columns/rows toward matching boundary segment direction, preserving other cells.

## Test instance
11x7, bg5. Perimeter color0: rightmost column rows0-2; leftmost column rows4-6. Two seed pixels color7 at (r4,c3),(r5,c3) zero-based. Other cells background 5. Eight submissions all incorrect; do not reuse guessed output blindly. Guesses tried included: painting rows from seed to edge left/right; changing seeds to 4; filling surrounding cells with 7. Need infer exact axis/direction/ray based on demos before solving recurrence. A likely relevant strategy is determine which perimeter segment each seed ray can align/aim at, and extend along straight unobstructed cardinal path, recoloring seeds to 4. Explicit feedback only said incorrect, not which cells.

Important process lesson: don't ramble / submit repetitive guesses. Parse demos as geometric rays from seed points extending toward matching perimeter boundary segments; identify color conversion (seed->4) and preserve all else. Keep exact dimensions/coordinates.

Input: background 8; left border c0 rows0..11 =7; right border c11 rows12..23=7. Color-9 source pixels at (13,3),(14,8),(16,5),(17,9),(18,7),(23,1). Input: bg9; top-left edge pair (r0,c0-1)=5,5; bottom-right pair (r4,c4-5)=5,5; source 0 at r1,c4. Output: source becomes 4 at r1,c4; color0 at r1,c0, r2,c0 and c4, r3,c0 and c4. Edge pairs preserved. This is evidence for 0-colored rays transferred via pair, with source marked 4.

Several attempted outputs all failed; do not reuse blindly. Initial hypothesis inserted rays down source column and through bottom pair; failed. # Continual-ARC

Check the diagonal direction and phase explicitly; do not infer a general rule from a coincidental overlap or merely replace apparent gaps.
3. When multiple rules fit, request a demo that distinguishes them, especially before the first guess or after a wrong submission. Choose what to disambiguate explicitly (e.g. copy source into adjacent panel vs all panels, reflect vs translate, or replicate across a divider vs only fill the displayed repeat). A demo's matching dimensions/colors alone is not sufficient; verify its exact transformation signature and which regions remain unchanged. Treat the demo as evidence about the transformation, not as a template for color substitution: derive the rule from aligned input/output cells, including background and all marker colors, and check whether the demonstrated relation actually applies to the test before constructing an output.
4. Before submitting, construct and validate the complete grid: row count, each row width, allowed colors, every changed cell, and unchanged regions. Submit only when the transformation is supported; use `finish` only after the instance is over.
